title: Re'eh: see the choice (Deuteronomy 11:26)
hookLine: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse"

lines: CHOICES THAT DON'T FEEL LIKE CHOICES.
cards: Some of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices while they're being made. Nobody decides to stop calling a brother. It just slowly happens.
Nobody chooses two hours of scrolling. They just don't choose not to. Psychologists have names for it: defaults, habits, autopilot.
Life comes at you as a stream, and the forks in the road go by without signs. The new portion opens by stopping that stream. Before it says a word about what to choose, it tells you to look.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse." The first word, behold, is re'eh in Hebrew. See.
It gives the portion its name. And there's a small oddity some commentators point out. Re'eh is singular: see, you, one person.

teach.h: SEE, YOU. BEFORE ALL OF YOU.
teach.b: But before you is plural: all of you. A whole people stands there, and each one is told to see for themselves. Nobody can look for you.
Then the choice is laid out plainly. The blessing, if you listen to the commandments; the curse, if you turn aside. And Moses gives it a geography.
When you cross the Jordan, set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, two real mountains.
Later, in the book of Joshua, the people do exactly that: half of them in front of one mountain, half in front of the other, and the blessing and the curse read aloud.
A choice you can stand between and see with your eyes.
And then two small words: this day. Not once, at Sinai, settled for good. Today, set before you again.
Some Jewish teachers hear in it a basic idea: that a person is free, and the road forks every day.
The Torah doesn't pretend the choice is easy, or that it's always obvious. It asks for something earlier and simpler. See it.
Notice that there's a fork at all.

how: Re'eh is read in synagogues in late summer, usually around the start of the month of Elul, when the season of reflection and self-examination before the High Holy Days begins.

o: see: the first word, said to each one
hear: the call to listen together
choose: the command to pick a road

s: re'eh is addressed to the whole crowd in the plural
re'eh is singular; before you is plural. each one sees for themselves.
the blessing and curse were tied to two real mountains
Gerizim for the blessing, Ebal for the curse.
the people actually carried out the ceremony later
in the book of Joshua, half the people stood in front of each mountain.

games.q: Moses sets a blessing and a curse before the people. before saying what to choose, what's the first thing he asks?
games.why: re'eh: behold, see. the choice starts with noticing that there's a fork at all.

practice: Walk through the rest of your day in your mind, hour by hour, and find one fork you'd normally slide past: the first thing you pick up, what you say when you walk in the door, whether you answer that message.
Picture the two mountains facing each other right there. You don't have to decide anything; just mark the spot.

wordCard.voice: Re'eh. See, or behold. Said to one person, in front of everyone: the first word and the name of the portion.

orig.note: Hebrew: see, behold. singular, though spoken to all Israel.

carryVoice: Your line: see the choice. A week that went beyond the letter, lived by more than bread, credited other hands, asked simply, opened the heart, and loved the stranger. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse
